en: CUL Or. 722.4 is a single-folio fragment of the beginning of a *sādhana*.
CUL Add. 1697.7 is a complete manuscript; the text was also input from there.

It is the *Vajraḍākastotradaṇḍaka* (*Dpal rdo rje mkha’ ’gro’i bstod pa rgyun chags*), Toh. no. 1442, Dergé Tanjur, vol. WA, folios 242r.4–243v.6. Translated by Maṇikaśrījñāna and Dpal gyi mtha’ can (i.e., Chos rje dpal).

In the language of India: *Śrī-vajraḍāka-stotra-dandaka-nāma*. In the language of Tibet: *Dpal rdo rje mkha' 'gro'i bstod pa rgyun chags shes bya ba* (The Continuous Praise to the Glorious Vajraḍāka). Homage to the glorious Cakrasaṃvara!
Homage to Śrī Cakrasaṃvara!

[He is] dark blue like a garland of *kuvalaya* petals, clouds, and *tamāla* trees, and the stainless sky; seated upon a vast lotus throne atop the Golden Mountain (Meru), which stands above the great circles of wind, fire, water, and earth; with the head of Śarva (Śiva) stepped upon and the pair of breasts of Gaurī mounted; [he is] one who causes the multitude of gods beginning with Upendra, Sūrya, Indra, and Candra to tremble; who terrifies many hosts of Daityas; the protector of the world; the remover of all doubt; clad in a tiger-skin garment; difficult to perform [his deeds] and difficult to cross [his power].

The entire sky was filled with the sounds of *hūṃ*, *phet*, and *hā hā* uttered by the courageous and profound ones; his crest was adorned with a universal vajra and a half-moon; he had utterly destroyed the darkness of delusion; he possessed a beautiful necklace of great conch shells; his two arms shone as they embraced the non-dual [consort], who is the nature of emptiness and non-dual gnosis; and he was endowed with a blazing vajra-bell... [the remainder is lost].

...embracing a woman who is his own nature; wearing the skin of a rutting elephant as a garment; with two hands busily holding a battle-axe, a trident, a fierce knife, a blazing vajra, a *khaṭvāṅga*, and a noose, together with a radiant human skull and a vessel for the sacrificial fire; shining with trembling arms that consume great flesh and fat; meditative, crowned, wise, and rich in intellect; possessing sixteen half-and-half faces, three eyes, and pure as a sacred ornament; adorned with a garland of human skulls; terrifying.
I pay homage to Vajrasattva, who ferries one across the terrible wilderness of saṃsāra and is the forest for the destruction of Māra. || 1 ||

Upon a golden mountain situated atop the mandalas of wind, fire, water, and earth, resting on a seat of a blossoming lotus, he sits upon the supreme blue sky—stainless like a garland of blue utpala clouds. He tramples Īśvara and presses down with equal force upon the two breasts of Gaurī, overwhelming Indra, Upendra, the fish, the moon, and other deities, while terrifying many asuras.

Performing [his deeds] and protecting the world, he strips away all fears; clad in a tiger-skin garment, he liberates the wicked. Firm and profound, he is of the nature of the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*. Filling all space with the roar of *hā hā*, he is marked by the crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) and the half-moon. With the supreme *uṣṇīṣa* that destroys the darkness of ignorance, he perfectly delivers beings. He possesses the great conch garland and the vajra sound of the bell.

Embraced by the mudrā of supreme clarity, he is the nature of the limb of passion—the non-dual primordial wisdom—accompanied by his noble consort. His two hands are bound by the garment of the hide of a great, intoxicated elephant; they brandish a blazing, radiant *kartṛ* (cleaver) and curved knife, a *khaṭvāṅga* with a spreading vajra, a lasso, a skull of Brahmā, and a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*).

Homage to Vajrasattva! He is adorned with hands from which skulls radiate; he partakes of flesh and great quantities of fat; he possesses meditative concentration, a crown, primordial wisdom, and the jewel of intelligence. With sixteen faces, each half-moon-shaped, and three eyes that purify all, he is adorned with garlands of human heads. Terrifying, fierce, and unbearable, he perfectly delivers beings from the wilderness of saṃsāra and subdues the Māras.
Homage to him!

Thereafter, he is joined by the four petals of the lotus and so forth, accompanied by Mahāḍākinī, Lāmikā, Khaṇḍarohā, Manohāriṇī, and Rūpiṇī; surrounded by skull-cups situated in the corners; then, the possessor of the excellent wheel of the circle of Vīras and Vīreśvarīs flashing with the reality of the conduct of the underworld, earth, and heaven located within the wheels of body, speech, and mind; worshipped by the eight goddesses beginning with Kākatuṇḍā stationed in the cardinal and intermediate directions; and charmingly embracing his own goddesses while displaying the expansion of the wondrous subjugation of Māra’s army and being impassioned for the sake of sentient beings.

He who hates hatred, who is intensely wrathful toward anger, who is a mass of afflictions, whose mind is intoxicated by drinking the wine of passion for the Māra of Death and others; who stands intent on the sole task of the three worlds, exalted in his Buddha-activity; whose limbs are covered with horripilation born from the touch of the face of the Vajra Goddess; whose lotus-eyes are flickering; who laughs with a whistling sound from the hollows of his throat; whose neck is raised and bound by the noose-like arms of his beloved; and who is fashioned amidst a shower of drops of joy arising from the tips of the hairs on her pair of high, full breasts.

Vajraḍāka, the eternal leader, who pervades the circle of the directions with a radiance like ten million suns, adorned with earrings, possessing the sprout-like fangs of a crescent moon, resplendent, bestowing glory, bestowing wisdom, granting nourishment, granting contentment, granting sovereignty, granting accomplishment, and bringing about all prosperity.

Following that, seated upon the four petals of the lotus are the great ḍākinīs, such as Lāmā, Khecarī, Saṃbhogā, and Manoharā, together with those who dwell in the intermediate directions and are encircled by skull-cups. Then, residing within the wheels of body, speech, and mind, they are the wrathful heroes and heroines, the lords of the three realms—those who move beneath the earth, upon the earth, and in the heavens.

The noble Cakrin is worshipped by the eight goddesses with the faces of vultures and so forth, who dwell in the cardinal and intermediate directions; endowed with the grace of union with his own consort, he strikes terror into the hosts of Māra. Radiant and perfectly attached to sentient beings, he destroys hatred, wrath, universal anger, and the afflictions—the Lord of Death himself.

With hearts satisfied by drinking the warm blood of Māra and his hosts, you remain as the sole performer of deeds throughout the three worlds. Born from the touch of the bliss of the Buddha-activity-vajra goddesses, your body is covered by throngs of horripilating hairs; with the lashes of your eyes quivering, you laugh with a "sid" sound from the hollow of your throat, while your lovely noose-like arms embrace the necks of those whose two breasts are full.

Worshiped by a multitude of droplets of dust arising from the firm foundation, its radiance pervades the various circles of the directions with the light of ten million suns; adorned with ornaments, its youthful crescent-moon fangs shimmer; it bestows glory, bestows wisdom, bestows satisfaction, bestows expansion, bestows sovereignty, and bestows accomplishments—all perfections.
I perpetually bow down to the Vajra Ḍākinī, the guide who bestows the supreme [attainment].

By the power of the majesty of incomparable compassion, he has shattered the entire array of the Tathāgatas; he has extinguished the flames of the blazing fire of the waves of afflictions that have entered the terrible ocean of *saṃsāra*; he is radiant with flashes of lightning intensified by faith; through the influence of his mass of gnosis, he has revealed the true nature of infinite phenomena. He perceives existence as non-existence, being as non-being, and the manifested nature of the three realms as his own form—formless, having destroyed all forms, abiding in the four Brahma-abodes, and adorned with the primary marks.

Refined by the consonants, it abides for the sake of benefiting sentient beings pervaded by the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*. It is the *oṃ* of the three principles, red with great passion, deluded by the wickedness of great hatred and great ignorance, and greedy with great craving. It is the consciousness that pervades the three worlds in a single moment—united with compassion and emptiness, having abandoned the two extremes of past and future—and which, through these glories, is the beautiful mass of bliss of the glorious Śrībhava. Purified by generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth, it is the external and internal cause of the world, terrifying, fierce, and dark.

He who takes on causes, whose appearance is terrifying, who crosses over hundreds of afflictions, who transcends form, whose body is subtle yet possesses a vast physical frame, the all-pervasive, the omnipresent, the meditative, the eternal, the one-eyed, the stationary, the moving, the immovable, the radiant, the hero among heroes, the Lord of the World through every mode of being. || 3 ||

Entering through the experience of incomparable compassion, the array of the Tathāgata radiates without exception, utterly destroying the surging garlands of waves of afflictions within the unbearable ocean of saṃsāra. Having perfectly displayed the pervasive rays of light from the mass of wisdom—blazing with a brilliance exceeding a thousand flaming fires and flashing with lightning—the self-nature of infinite phenomena...

Free from substantiality, yet arising from the essence of non-substantiality; the nature of the three realms, beautiful in form yet free from all forms, having utterly transcended form; dwelling steadfastly in the four Brahma-abodes; adorned with the primary marks and beautifully embellished with the secondary signs; pervading the three bodies—the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa—such is the activity for the benefit of sentient beings, which is itself the three [bodies].

Attachment to passion is not great; aversion toward the unwholesome is great; delusion is great; craving for desire is great. Compassion is non-dual with emptiness. Having abandoned the extremes of the past and the future, the three worlds are pervaded in a single instant. With the manifestation of consciousness, the supreme assembly of great joy is beautiful; it bestows purity in generosity, ethical discipline, and so forth, [dispelling] the outer and inner darkness.

He who performs deeds that cross over and traverse the unbearable, the ravisher who truly delivers one from the fears of saṃsāra, the plunderer of all afflictions and secondary afflictions; he who possesses form and gathers all forms, who terrifies all the malevolent, whose subtle body is vast and whose great body is immense; the pervasive lord, the all-pervading, the eternal, the momentary, the stable, the moving, the luminous, the hero, and the heroine.
I bow with all my being to Īśvara, the Lord of the World.

In that place, which was terrifying with the fires of many loathsome corpses piled up; adorned with fierce fragments of bones, eggs, hair, and the like; slippery with masses of mud from the marrow and brains of heads being burned; covered with garlands of severed hair and entrails; illuminated by the "hā hā" cries of *ḍākinīs*, spirits, and *vetālas*; formidable with the many "huṃ" sounds of practitioners; filled with the tumultuous howling of prowling jackals; crowded with rows of skeletons dancing with arms outstretched; and arising from the overflow of the drinking of heroes—

Having praised with words the Guru Heruka, who dances amidst the eight cremation grounds in every direction and intermediate point—where a multitude of lordly yoginīs and yogīs exult in noble dance due to the sweetness of the *ānanda-saṃgīti*; where the darkness is thickened by streams of blood flowing from limbs severed and struck by the vulture’s beak; which is turbid with the garlands of flickering flames from the most fierce fire issuing from the mouth of Śiva; and which is formidable with the army of Kāla at the shore of Mahākāla—may this person, by the merit produced as it spreads throughout the expanse of the realm of space, pierce through the mountain of ignorance.

May he—who, having torn asunder the incomparable web of afflictions, has brought forth the accumulation of stainless gnosis consisting of a mass of merit; who manifests a radiance that is the light of non-arising, illuminating the entire universe and utterly dispelling the darkness of infinite delusion; and who, like a thunderbolt, performs in a single moment the sole task of all the perfectly awakened ones—may he remain forever and in every way. 4.

Smeared with marrow, possessing a form of many marvelous and terrifying aspects, the corpse-eater has fierce fire for a mouth; he is adorned with severed human heads, fierce bones, and heaps of bone fragments, as well as hair and the like. As he burns, his supreme limbs drip with brains, and he smears himself with fat and marrow. With severed hair and dangling garlands of intestines, he is surrounded by ḍākinīs, bhūtas, and vetālas.

Uttering loud cries of "ha ha," the practitioners should threaten with the syllable *hūṃ*, shout out the sounds of *pheṃ* and *phaṭ*, raise their hands, and perform dances. With joy arising from the exhilaration of the heroes' drink, they should sing melodious songs and dance, moving and sporting as a gathering of lords of yogins and yoginīs.

With the blood-streams dripping from bodies seized and torn by the beaks of vultures, and amidst masses of fiercely blazing fire emerging from the mouths of jackals, you perform the dance within hundreds of divine charnel grounds—dark, dense with the gathered hosts of Māra at the great time of destruction—to the Guru Heruka; through the merit of my verbal offerings, may [this] fill the expanse of space.

Through this supreme birth, having abandoned the entire web of afflictions of these births and accumulated an incomparable mass of merit, the stainless accumulation of supreme primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) was manifested. Illuminated by the light of perfect self-awareness, in a single instant, the infinite darkness of ignorance regarding the manifold variety was completely dispelled;
thus, one becomes forever like the body of all the Vajraḍākinīs and the perfect Buddhas.
The *Śrīcakrasaṃvaradaṇḍakastuti* is completed.
The *Śrīvajraḍākinīstotra-santati*, known as the "Continuous Praise," composed by the great master, the crown jewel of the assembly of logicians, the glorious Dharmakīrti, is hereby complete.
Translated, edited, and finalized by the Indian preceptor Maṇikarśijñāna in the presence of the Tibetan translator, the Śākya bhikṣu named Dpal-gyi-mtha’ (Śrīpāda).

Regarding the extent of this text, in the manuscript of the Guru, each four-line stanza consists of thirty-six syllables; thus, when all four stanzas are totaled, there are one thousand three hundred and forty-four syllables. In the Tibetan manuscript, however, each line contains two hundred and ninety-five *tseg* (word-dividers), totaling one thousand one hundred and eighty *tseg*.
